title: U.S. Senate · Mississippi

context.text: This is the Class II Senate seat held by Cindy Hyde-Smith, who first took office in 2018. Hyde-Smith defeated Sarah Adlakha in the March 10, 2026 Republican primary, 80.8% to 19.2%. Scott Colom defeated Priscilla W. Till and Albert Littell in the Democratic primary, 72.9% to 18.6% to 8.5%. Ty Pinkins is running as an independent.

summary.text: Cindy Hyde-Smith is the Republican incumbent U.S. Senator from Mississippi, seeking a second full term. A cattle farmer from Brookhaven, she served in the Mississippi State Senate (2000-2012) and as state Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce (2012-2018) before Gov. Phil Bryant appointed her to the seat of retiring Sen. Thad Cochran in 2018. She won the 2018 special election and a full term in 2020, and sits on the Appropriations, Agriculture, Energy and Natural Resources, and Rules committees.

background.text: Born in Brookhaven, Mississippi, and grew up in Monticello, Mississippi.
Graduated from Copiah-Lincoln Community College and the University of Southern Mississippi, where she earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and political science.
Worked as a lobbyist and congressional affairs consultant before returning to Mississippi and running for the state legislature, according to Ballotpedia and Wikipedia.

Elected to the Mississippi State Senate in 1999 and served District 39 from 2000 to 2012, including eight years as chair of the Agriculture Committee. She was elected as a Democrat and switched her party affiliation to Republican in December 2010.
Elected Mississippi Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce in 2011, taking office in January 2012, and re-elected in 2015; she was the first woman to hold the post.

Appointed to the U.S. Senate by Gov. Phil Bryant on April 2, 2018, to fill the seat vacated by Thad Cochran, becoming the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress. She won the November 2018 special election runoff against Mike Espy and was elected to a full term in 2020, again defeating Espy.

In the 119th Congress serves on the Appropriations, Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, Energy and Natural Resources, and Rules and Administration committees, and chairs the Appropriations subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development and the Agriculture subcommittee on Commodities, Derivatives, Risk Management, and Trade.

According to her Senate office, the first bill she introduced as a senator, a migratory bird hunting-season measure for youth, veterans and active military, became law in March 2019 as part of a larger package; she also leads the Senate Pro-Life Caucus.
According to her Senate biography, she and her husband Mike have a daughter, live in Brookhaven, and her family raises beef cattle and is a partner in a local stockyard auction market.

priorities.text: Supports federal policies to foster economic growth and job creation in Mississippi, including the 2017 tax cuts.
Supports the state's agriculture and forestry industries, citing her background as a cattle farmer and former state agriculture commissioner.

positions.summary: Holds an enhanced-carry permit and describes herself as a strong advocate for the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms.

candidates.name: Scott Colom
candidates.currentRole: District Attorney, Mississippi 16th Circuit Court District

summary.text: Scott Colom is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate and the elected District Attorney of Mississippi's 16th Circuit Court District (Clay, Lowndes, Noxubee and Oktibbeha counties). A Columbus native and former Mississippi Center for Justice staff lawyer, municipal judge and city prosecutor, he was elected district attorney in 2015 and was twice nominated by President Biden to a federal district court seat, though the Senate did not confirm him. He won the March 10, 2026 Democratic primary with 72.9% of the vote.

background.text: Born December 24, 1982, in Columbus, Mississippi, where he was raised. According to his campaign website, he is a seventh-generation Mississippian and the son of retired Judge Dorothy Colom, the first African American elected to her region's Chancery Court, and attorney Wilbur Colom.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Millsaps College in 2005 and a J.D., cum laude, from the University of Wisconsin Law School in 2009.
From 2009 to 2011 was a staff lawyer and Skadden Fellow at the Mississippi Center for Justice, then ran the Colom Law Firm from 2011 to 2016.
Served as an interim Lowndes County justice court judge and as a municipal court judge in Aberdeen (2012-2013), and as city prosecutor in Columbus (2013-2016).
Elected District Attorney of the 16th Judicial District in 2015, defeating the longtime incumbent, and sworn in January 4, 2016; he was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and won re-election in 2023.

As district attorney, handled cases including the 2021 dismissal of murder charges against Eddie Lee Howard, who had spent 23 years on death row on a conviction that relied on bite-mark evidence, and several cold-case prosecutions, according to Wikipedia.

Nominated by President Biden on October 14, 2022, to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi and renominated in January 2023; the Senate did not confirm him and the nomination was returned to the President on January 3, 2024.
Announced his Senate candidacy in September 2025. According to his campaign website, he and his wife Nadia have two daughters, and he is a member of Missionary Union Baptist Church in Columbus.

priorities.text: Says he is running to lower costs for Mississippi families.
Says he wants to save Mississippi's rural hospitals.
Says he wants to bring jobs home to Mississippi.

positions.summary: Campaign site lists saving Mississippi's rural hospitals as a core priority.

summary.text: Ty Pinkins is an independent candidate for U.S. Senate. A Rolling Fork, Mississippi native, he is an attorney and 21-year U.S. Army veteran who served as a White House Communications Agency aide, then attended Georgetown Law on the G.I. Bill. He was the Democratic nominee for Mississippi Secretary of State in 2023 and for U.S. Senate in 2024, and is running this year without a party.

background.text: Born in Rolling Fork, Mississippi; in a Ballotpedia survey he says he grew up there in a working-class family.
Served in the U.S. Army from 1996 to 2017, which he describes as 21 years including three combat tours.
Worked as a presidential communications aide with the White House Communications Agency, serving, he says, under both Democratic and Republican presidents.

Earned a bachelor's degree in political science and government from the University of Maryland Global Campus (2012), a J.D. from Georgetown University Law Center (2020), and a master's degree in national security law from Georgetown (2021).
His career experience includes owning a business and working as an attorney with the Mississippi Center for Justice; he describes himself as a Mississippi attorney and author.
Ran as the Democratic nominee for Mississippi Secretary of State in 2023, losing to incumbent Michael Watson 59.5% to 40.5%.
Was the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in 2024, losing to incumbent Roger Wicker 62.8% to 37.2%.

priorities.text: Says the two-party system has "stopped working for too many Americans" and is running as an independent so Mississippi has "a senator who answers to the people, not party bosses or political establishments."
priorities.quote: Both major parties have failed working people. My campaign is rooted in the belief that the two-party system has stopped working for too many Americans.

priorities.text: Says he is passionate about expanding access to affordable healthcare, especially in rural areas.
Says he wants to ensure veterans receive the benefits, care, and support they earned.

positions.summary: Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey lists expanding access to affordable healthcare, especially in rural areas, as a passion.
